b.v: About 25 minutes. Everything on this page runs in your browser - nothing to install.
1) print
print() puts something on the screen. That is the whole of it. Press Run and see.

python
print("Hello")
print("My name is Khalid")
Now change the name to yours and press Run again. The box is yours to edit - break it, fix it, that is what it is for.
2) Variables
A variable is a name for a value. You make one by writing the name, an equals sign, and the value. No keyword, no type, no declaration.

python
name = "Ayesha"
age = 30

print(name)
print(age)
If you did the VBA course: this is Dim name As String followed by name = "Ayesha", except Python skips the Dim. It works out the type from what you put in.
3) The equals sign is not equality
x = 5 does not claim that x equals five. It puts five into x. You can put something else in a moment later, and the old value is gone.

python
x = 5
print(x)

x = 10
print(x)

x = x + 1
print(x)
That last line looks like nonsense as mathematics - x cannot be x plus one. As an instruction it is fine: take what is in x, add one, put it back.
4) Naming things

v: Letters, numbers and underscores only
Cannot start with a number
Case matters - name and Name are two different variables
By habit, lower case with underscores: first_name, not FirstName

b.v: Case matters more than beginners expect. print(Name) when you made name will not quietly use the wrong one - it will stop with an error saying Name is not defined. That is Python being helpful.
5) Your first error
Run this. It is broken on purpose.

python
print("one")
print(tow)
print("three")
Read the last line of the message: NameError, name 'tow' is not defined. Python is saying it has never heard of tow. Notice also that one printed and three did not - Python stops at the error.
Always read the last line of an error first. The rest is the path that led there, and beginners waste a lot of time reading it top to bottom.
6) Comments

python
# Anything after a hash is ignored
price = 250   # so is this
print(price)
In VBA a comment starts with an apostrophe. In Python it is a hash. Same purpose: notes for humans, invisible to the machine.

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) Arithmetic

python
print(10 + 3)
print(10 - 3)
print(10 * 3)
print(10 / 3)
print(10 // 3)
print(10 % 3)
print(10 ** 3)

v: / = ordinary division, always gives a decimal
// = division with the remainder thrown away
% = only the remainder
** = to the power of

b.v: % is more useful than it looks. n % 2 is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd, which is how you test for even without any special function.
2) Two kinds of number

python
print(type(7))
print(type(7.5))
print(7 / 1)
int is a whole number, float has a decimal point. Notice 7 / 1 gives 7.0 and not 7 - division always produces a float, even when it comes out even.
3) Text
Text is called a string. Single or double quotes, it does not matter, as long as you finish with the one you started with.

python
first = "Ali"
last = "Khan"

print(first + " " + last)
print(first * 3)
print(len(first))
Plus joins strings. Star repeats one. len() counts the characters.
4) The mistake everyone makes
Run this. It fails, and the reason matters.

python
age = "30"
print(age + 5)
"30" in quotes is text, not a number. You cannot add 5 to it any more than you could add 5 to the word thirty. Python says so plainly: can only concatenate str to str.

python
age = "30"
print(int(age) + 5)

count = 7
print("I have " + str(count) + " books")
int() turns text into a number, str() turns a number into text. When something refuses to work with numbers and text together, this is nearly always why.
5) f-strings, the tidy way

python
name = "Sana"
age = 25

print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print(f"Next year she will be {age + 1}")
Put an f before the quote and anything inside curly brackets gets worked out and dropped in. No str(), no plus signs. Use this everywhere - it is what real Python looks like.
In VBA you would write "I have " & count & " books". The f-string is the same idea, done more neatly.
6) Useful string tricks

python
s = "  Hello World  "

print(s.strip())
print(s.upper())
print(s.lower())
print(s.strip().replace("World", "Lahore"))
print("one,two,three".split(","))

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) if
Change 20 to 15 and run it again. Note the colon at the end of the if line, and the four spaces on the line below.
2) The indentation is the grammar
Most languages mark a block with brackets or a word like End If. Python uses the indent itself. Lines pushed in belong to the if; lines back at the margin do not.

python
x = 5

if x > 3:
    print("inside the if")
    print("also inside")
print("outside, always runs")
This is the one thing that catches everybody. Four spaces per level, and be consistent - mixing tabs and spaces gives errors that are hard to see because they look identical on screen.
VBA has If ... Then ... End If. Python has no End If - the indent already said where the block stopped. Fewer words, but the spacing now matters.
3) Comparing

python
print(5 == 5)
print(5 != 5)
print(5 > 3)
print(5 <= 4)
print("abc" == "abc")
One equals sets a value. Two equals asks a question. x = 5 puts five in x; x == 5 asks whether it is already five. Getting these the wrong way round is the most common bug in any language.
4) More than two paths
elif is else-if. Python checks each in turn and stops at the first true one. Order matters - put 60 first and every mark above 60 would get a C.
5) and, or, not
Python uses the plain English words, not && and ||. and needs both sides true; or needs one.
6) What counts as false
Empty text, zero, and an empty list all count as false. So if name: reads as if there is a name, which is shorter than comparing to an empty string and is what Python programmers actually write.

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) for and range
It printed 0 1 2 3 4 - five numbers, starting at zero, stopping before five. range(5) means five of them, not up to five. This trips up everyone once.
range(start, stop) begins where you say. range(start, stop, step) counts in jumps. The stop is never included.
2) Looping over text
A for loop walks through anything with parts - text, lists, and more you will meet tomorrow. You are not limited to counting.
3) while

python
count = 3

while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1

print("Go")
while keeps going as long as its condition holds. Use for when you know how many times; use while when you do not.
Forget the count = count - 1 line and the condition never becomes false. That is an endless loop. The box on this page stops after three seconds, but on your own computer it would sit there forever.
4) Try breaking it
Run this and watch it get stopped.

python
count = 3

while count > 0:
    print(count)

print("never reached")
Now add count = count - 1 inside the loop and run it again.
5) break and continue

v: break = leave the loop now
continue = skip the rest of this turn, go round again

b.v: If you did VBA: for is For ... Next, while is Do While ... Loop, and break is Exit For. Same ideas, shorter words.
6) A loop worth keeping

python
total = 0

for n in range(1, 101):
    total = total + n

print(f"1 to 100 adds up to {total}")

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) A list

python
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]

print(fruits)
print(len(fruits))
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[2])
Counting starts at zero. The first item is [0] and the third is [2]. Asking for fruits[3] in a list of three gives an IndexError - there is no fourth.
2) Counting from the back

python
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]

print(fruits[-1])
print(fruits[-2])
Minus one is the last item, always, whatever the length. Much better than working out len(fruits) - 1 every time.
3) Changing a list

python
nums = [3, 1, 4]

nums.append(9)
print(nums)

nums.insert(0, 7)
print(nums)

nums.remove(1)
print(nums)

last = nums.pop()
print(last, nums)
4) Sorting and searching

python
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]

print(sorted(nums))
print(sorted(nums, reverse=True))
print(max(nums), min(nums), sum(nums))
print(9 in nums)
print(3 in nums)
sorted() gives you a new sorted list and leaves the original alone. nums.sort() changes the original instead. Both are useful; know which one you called.
5) Looping over a list

python
prices = [120, 340, 90, 560]
total = 0

for p in prices:
    total = total + p

print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Average: {total / len(prices)}")

python
names = ["Ali", "Sana", "Bilal"]

for i, name in enumerate(names, start=1):
    print(f"{i}. {name}")
enumerate gives you the position and the item together, which saves keeping a counter by hand.
6) Slicing

python
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]

print(letters[1:3])
print(letters[:2])
print(letters[2:])
print(letters[-2:])
Two numbers with a colon take a slice: from the first, up to but not including the second. Leave one out and Python assumes the start or the end.

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) When a list is the wrong shape
A list holds things in order and you fetch them by number. But if you want the price of sugar, counting to the right position is silly. You want to ask by name.

python
prices = {"sugar": 180, "rice": 340, "oil": 560}

print(prices["rice"])
print(len(prices))
Curly brackets, and each entry is a key, a colon, then a value. The key is what you look up by.
2) Adding and changing

python
prices = {"sugar": 180}

prices["tea"] = 750
prices["sugar"] = 195

print(prices)
del prices["tea"]
print(prices)
Assigning to a key that exists changes it. Assigning to one that does not adds it. There is no separate add.
3) Asking for something that is not there
KeyError. Python will not invent a value. When you are not sure, use get instead.

python
prices = {"sugar": 180}

print(prices.get("salt"))
print(prices.get("salt", 0))
print("salt" in prices)
get with a second argument is the tidy way to say use this if it is missing. It comes up constantly once you work with real data.
4) Looping over a dictionary
Looping plainly gives you the keys. .items() gives you both halves, which is nearly always what you want.
5) Something real
6) A dictionary inside a dictionary
Inside an f-string, use the other kind of quote for the key - info['role'] with single quotes inside double. Same quote twice ends the string early.

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write your own function
Pass values in and get one back
Stop repeating yourself

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) Why
When the same few lines appear three times, any change means finding all three. A function gives those lines a name, and then there is one place to change.

python
def greet():
    print("Hello there")

greet()
greet()
def makes it, the brackets and colon end the line, and the indented lines are the body. Nothing happens until you call it by name.
2) Giving it something to work with

python
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello {name}")

greet("Ali")
greet("Sana")
3) Getting something back

python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 4)
print(result)
print(add(10, 20))

print shows a value on the screen. return hands it back to whoever called. A function that prints but does not return gives you None, and you cannot do sums with it. This distinction confuses people for weeks.

python
def shows(n):
    print(n * 2)

def gives(n):
    return n * 2

a = shows(5)
b = gives(5)

print(f"a is {a}")
print(f"b is {b}")
print(gives(5) + 1)
4) Defaults

python
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting} {name}"

print(greet("Ali"))
print(greet("Ali", "Salam"))
A default is used when the caller leaves that one out. Defaults must come after the arguments that have none.
5) Something worth keeping

python
def gst(amount, rate=18):
    tax = amount * rate / 100
    return amount + tax

print(gst(1000))
print(gst(1000, 5))

for price in [500, 1200, 8000]:
    print(f"{price} -> {gst(price)}")

If you did VBA: def is Function, and return is the same idea as setting the function name equal to a value. VBA also has Sub for the ones that give nothing back - Python does not bother with the distinction.
6) Where names live

python
total = 100

def change():
    total = 5
    print(f"inside: {total}")

change()
print(f"outside: {total}")
The total inside the function is its own. Setting it does not touch the one outside. That is deliberate - a function should not quietly change things around it.

v: Read an error properly
Catch one instead of crashing

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) The four common ones

python
print(undefined_thing)

python
print("5" + 5)

python
items = [1, 2, 3]
print(items[5])

v: NameError = you used a name Python has never seen
TypeError = you mixed two kinds of thing that do not mix
IndexError = you asked for a position past the end
KeyError = you asked for a key the dictionary has not got

b.v: The last line names the problem and the line number. Read that first. Everything above it is the route Python took to get there, and beginners lose a lot of time reading it from the top.
2) Catching one

python
try:
    n = int("hello")
    print(n)
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a number")

print("still running")
Without the try, the program stops there. With it, the except runs instead and the rest carries on.
3) Where it belongs
Wrap the one line that might fail, not the whole program. A try around everything hides real bugs and makes them much harder to find later.
Never write a bare except: with nothing after it. It swallows every error including your own typing mistakes, and you will spend an evening hunting a problem the computer was ready to tell you about.
4) Dividing by zero
5) Checking first
Often a simple check is clearer than catching an error. Use try for things you cannot check in advance - a file that might not open, text that might not be a number.

1) The shape real data takes
A list of dictionaries is how almost every real dataset arrives - rows of records, each with named fields. A spreadsheet in Python's shape.
2) Totals
3) Filtering

python
sales = [
    {"item": "sugar", "qty": 3, "price": 180},
    {"item": "rice",  "qty": 2, "price": 340},
    {"item": "oil",   "qty": 1, "price": 560},
    {"item": "tea",   "qty": 5, "price": 750}
]

big = []
for s in sales:
    if s["price"] > 300:
        big.append(s["item"])

print(big)

big2 = [s["item"] for s in sales if s["price"] > 300]
print(big2)
The second version is a list comprehension - the same loop written on one line. Read it as: this item, for each sale, where the price is over 300.
4) Sorting records

python
sales = [
    {"item": "sugar", "price": 180},
    {"item": "tea",   "price": 750},
    {"item": "rice",  "price": 340}
]

by_price = sorted(sales, key=lambda s: s["price"])
for s in by_price:
    print(f"{s['item']}: {s['price']}")

print("---")

dearest = max(sales, key=lambda s: s["price"])
print(f"Dearest: {dearest['item']}")
key tells sorted what to sort on. lambda s: s["price"] is a one-line function meaning take a sale and give me its price. Do not worry about lambda beyond this use - it is how sorting records is done.
5) Grouping
totals.get(city, 0) + amount is the whole trick: start at zero if this city is new, otherwise add to what is there. This one line replaces a lot of clumsy if-statements.

b.v: 2) A small shop report
Everything here is something you met in the last nine days. Read it, run it, then change the numbers.

python
sales = [
    {"item": "sugar", "qty": 3, "price": 180},
    {"item": "rice",  "qty": 2, "price": 340},
    {"item": "oil",   "qty": 1, "price": 560},
    {"item": "tea",   "qty": 5, "price": 750},
    {"item": "salt",  "qty": 4, "price": 60}
]

def line_total(sale):
    return sale["qty"] * sale["price"]

def with_gst(amount, rate=18):
    return amount + amount * rate / 100

print("ITEM        QTY   PRICE    TOTAL")
print("-" * 36)

grand = 0
for s in sales:
    t = line_total(s)
    grand = grand + t
    print(f"{s['item']:<10} {s['qty']:>3} {s['price']:>7} {t:>8}")

print("-" * 36)
print(f"{'Subtotal':<22} {grand:>13}")
print(f"{'With GST':<22} {with_gst(grand):>13.0f}")

biggest = max(sales, key=lambda s: line_total(s))
print(f"\nBiggest line: {biggest['item']}")
The {s['item']:<10} bits line the columns up - left-aligned in ten spaces, right-aligned in seven. That is all that makes it look like a table.
